title: Oracle Stock Crashes 65% From Peak as AI Spending Gamble Backfires
excerpt: S&P's credit downgrade to one notch above junk and a $638 billion backlog dominated by a single unprofitable customer have turned Oracle from Wall Street darling to cautionary tale.
body:
• Oracle shares have plunged roughly 65% from their September 2025 record high of $345.72, erasing more than $500 billion in market value.
  • S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle to BBB- in July 2026, placing the company one notch above junk status, citing high customer concentration and escalating capital expenditure.
  • About half of Oracle's $638 billion backlog comes from OpenAI, which has missed revenue targets and delayed its IPO.
  • Oracle's free cash flow swung to negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026 as it took on $43 billion in new debt to fund its AI data center buildout.

Oracle hit a fresh 52-week low on Monday, trading as low as $120.03 — its weakest level since April 2025 — as the once-celebrated AI infrastructure play continued its relentless decline. The stock has now shed roughly 65% from the record $345.72 it reached last September, when the company's $300 billion deal with OpenAI sent its market capitalisation soaring past $930 billion.

What was once the bull case is now the bear case. Oracle's $638 billion in remaining performance obligations — contracted future revenue that quadrupled year-on-year — looks less like a growth engine and more like a concentration risk after S&P Global Ratings cut the company's credit rating to BBB- last week, leaving it one notch above junk.

The OpenAI Problem

"Oracle's rapidly expanding AI infrastructure business is increasing its overall credit risk, reflecting our more cautious view of the AI infrastructure industry, including rising capital expenditure requirements, an uncertain path to profitability, rapidly evolving industry and competitive landscape, and high customer concentration," S&P wrote in its downgrade note, according to Investor's Business Daily.

The agency pointed to a single uncomfortable fact: OpenAI accounts for roughly half of Oracle's entire backlog. That customer is unprofitable, recently missed internal revenue and user-growth targets according to the Wall Street Journal, and has delayed its planned IPO — the very fundraising event that would have reassured investors about its ability to honour $300 billion in compute commitments.

"It was the halo around your proverbial head that's now the noose around your neck," Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group, told Marketplace. "People think some part of what OpenAI is committed to will not come to fruition."

Debt, Cash Burns, and a Shrinking Workforce

Oracle spent roughly $55.7 billion on capital projects in fiscal 2026 and posted a free cash flow deficit of negative $23.7 billion — a staggering deterioration from the $394 million deficit recorded just a year earlier. To finance the buildout, the company raised $43 billion in debt and $5 billion in equity during the fiscal year ended May, according to Reuters.

The spending is far from over. Oracle has flagged net capital expenditure of around $70 billion for its current fiscal year and plans to raise another $40 billion, including a $20 billion stock issuance that analysts estimate would dilute shareholders by roughly 4.8%. S&P now expects the company's fiscal 2027 cash flow deficit to widen to approximately negative $42 billion — nearly double its prior estimate.

Meanwhile, reports indicate more than 10,000 employees have already been laid off, with some analysts estimating the total could reach 30,000 as Oracle attempts to redirect resources toward its AI ambitions.

The Chinese AI Shadow

Adding to investor anxiety is the competitive threat from Chinese AI models. DeepSeek's breakthrough models, which perform comparably to OpenAI's offerings at a fraction of the training cost, have fuelled doubts about whether the massive AI infrastructure buildout is sustainable. If cheaper, more efficient models reduce the demand for raw compute power, the hundreds of billions being poured into data centres could yield diminishing returns.

"Oracle's accelerated data center buildout is pressuring near-term gross margins and raising investor questions around CapEx, funding, and returns."

— Citizens JMP Securities

CLSA initiated coverage of Oracle with a Hold rating this month, warning the company may need up to $500 billion to fund its AI cloud expansion through 2030 — with internal cash generation covering only a fraction of that amount.

A Bargain or a Value Trap?

After the rout, Oracle trades at roughly 16 times forward earnings with a 1.6% dividend yield, and its fiscal fourth-quarter results in June beat expectations. Revenue rose 22% to $67 billion for the full year, cloud infrastructure revenue jumped 84%, and the company guided for $90 billion in revenue for fiscal 2027.

But the gap between Oracle and its cloud rivals grows starker by the day. Microsoft carries a AAA credit rating, Alphabet sits at AA+, and Amazon at AA. Oracle is chasing the same contracts from seven to nine notches lower on the credit ladder, relying on borrowed money rather than internal cash flows to finance its ambitions.

The stock has closed higher in just four of its last 20 trading sessions, and is down 35% year to date. For Indian diaspora investors with exposure to US tech — whether through direct holdings, index funds, or 401(k) accounts — Oracle's trajectory is a stark reminder that contracted revenue is not the same as collected revenue, and that even the most compelling growth story can buckle under the weight of its own leverage.

What's Next

All eyes now turn to whether OpenAI can secure the funding needed to honour its commitments, and whether Oracle's data centre projects face further delays. New Mexico recently blocked a pipeline for Oracle's planned 2.5 GW data centre, and Wisconsin regulators are requiring the company to post $100 million in annual collateral due to its below-threshold credit rating. If the credit rating slips one more notch into speculative territory, the cost of Oracle's borrowing — and the viability of its entire AI bet — could fundamentally change.
